generation.hypothesis: Integrating in situ high-temperature TGA with synchrotron-based XRD will enable simultaneous observation and correlation of oxidation kinetics and phase evolution in high-temperature materials.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-temperature alloy or ceramic sample in its unoxidized state.
generation.intervention: Expose the material to controlled high-temperature oxidizing conditions in an integrated TGA-XRD experimental setup.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environment (several hundred degrees Celsius or above) under an oxidizing atmosphere where both significant mass change and phase transformations occur.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolving oxide layers and changing crystalline phases, which link mass gain (measured via TGA) with structural transitions (captured by XRD).
generation.mechanism: As the sample oxidizes, TGA records a mass increase while the synchrotron-based XRD simultaneously detects phase transitions. The temporal correlation between these two datasets will reveal how oxidation kinetics are directly related to phase stability and transformations.
generation.predicted_outcome: A synchronized dataset where the onset and rate of mass gain are accompanied by distinct changes in the diffraction pattern, thereby establishing a direct relationship between oxidation events and phase evolution.
generation.baseline: Previous methods that independently track oxidation (via TGA) and structural changes (via ex situ or separate in situ XRD), which do not provide real-time, correlated data.
generation.boundary: This integrated method may be limited for systems with extremely rapid oxidation kinetics or very subtle phase transitions where the temporal resolution of the instruments is insufficient to capture simultaneous dynamics.
generation.uncertainty: The degree of quantitative correlation between mass change and phase transformation may vary depending on the material system and oxidation rate; further calibration may be necessary to generalize the method.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare an unoxidized high-temperature alloy sample and load it into an integrated TGA-synchrotron XRD setup. Subject the sample to a controlled high-temperature oxidizing atmosphere while continuously recording both the mass change and the evolving XRD patterns.
measurements: Time-resolved synchrotron XRD patterns indicating phase transformations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If significant oxidation-induced mass changes are recorded without any corresponding alterations in the XRD patterns (or if phase changes occur without concurrent mass change), then the hypothesized direct correlation between oxidation kinetics and phase evolution is not captured, thereby falsifying the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].

Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. decision.trend: Early work in high-temperature materials largely employed ex situ approaches or separate in situ techniques (for example, using thermogravimetric analysis to record mass gains due to oxidation and X‐ray diffraction to assess phase changes) to study oxidation or phase evolution under high temperature. Studies such as PMC7475834 demonstrated coating evolution upon oxidation but analyzed the oxide layers post‐mortem, while PMC11077685 used in situ XRD during thermal processing yet tracked oxidation by independent means. These sequential or isolated measurements provided valuable insights but did not capture the interplay between oxidation kinetics and concurrent phase transformations.
decision.unsolved: A key gap remains in simultaneously and in situ capturing both the oxidation kinetics (mass change) and the evolution of phase stability during high-temperature exposure, which is essential to understand the dynamic interrelation between oxidation and phase transformations under realistic operating conditions.
decision.lever: Integrate in situ high-temperature thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) with synchrotron-based X-ray diffraction (XRD) in one experimental setup
decision.why: This combined method directly couples mass-change data with real-time diffraction data, thereby enabling simultaneous observation of oxidation kinetics and phase evolution. It builds on the separate approaches in earlier studies, addressing the limitation of lacking correlation between oxidation behavior and phase stability under high-temperature conditions.
